title: Part VII — PLATFORM: How Commerce Platforms Are Built

know: Part VII answers five questions in order: how software is divided into separately deployed programs and when a split pays; how vendors share infrastructure between customers and how API call budgets limit integrations; who owns each extension and what it may change; whether pages are rendered by the platform or by a separate headless application; and how to prepare the whole order path for a peak.

Kestrel & Pine's starting point: two early-2027 rebuild proposals (about €3.2M for separate commerce services, €240,000 for a separate storefront) while the platform held 2,300 orders in the 2026 peak hour, order export managed about seven a minute and stock lagged up to two hours.
That a merchant on a hosted platform rents the renderer, the checkout and a share of a multi-tenant system, and owns the theme, the apps and the integration code around them.

thesis.question: How does the way a bought platform is built limit what a merchant can promise, and what is left for the merchant to decide?
thesis.claim: The vendor builds and runs the inside (architecture style, pooled tenancy, extension points, renderer, peak capacity), which reaches the merchant as limits: API budgets the vendor may lower, extension points with retirement dates, a checkout the merchant cannot replace. Within them, the merchant's promises are kept or broken in what it owns around the platform: its integration code, its share of each budget, its apps, its page scripts and its order chain.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the platform's architecture decides what a merchant can promise, so a merchant whose promises fail should move to a more modern architecture: microservices, composable commerce, a headless storefront or a higher plan tier.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers rebuild, headless and 'are we behind?' proposals with measurements of its own layer, and governs what it owns before it replaces what it rents. On Black Friday 2026 Kestrel & Pine's platform held 2,300 orders in the peak hour while its order flow carried about seven orders a minute and stock reached the channels up to two hours late. In 2027 it declined a composable rebuild (about €3.2M) and a headless storefront (about €240,000), stayed on the platform (W4), kept its own code in one integration service, put the order flow first in its API budget, cut 41 apps to 34 with no app writing stock, brought INP from 310 ms to 180 ms for about €38,000 of agency time, and wrote a peak plan that tests every link at 80 orders a minute.
thesis.how_why: The vendor deploys the core for many merchants, so a merchant can neither change nor verify its internal style. What the merchant shares is capacity, which the vendor protects with fixed budgets it may shrink; the shared pool smooths the platform's own peak across tenants while each budget meets one merchant's spike in full. Extension points and API versions are retired on the vendor's dates, the platform keeps checkout, and every script the merchant adds to a page slows it. Everything the merchant adds (integration code, apps, scripts, flows) spends from those limits, and no vendor review sees how the merchant's additions combine, so each Kestrel & Pine failure this part examines crossed the merchant's own layer while the platform did what its vendor designed.

supporting_claims.claim: An architecture style is a choice of deployment units, data ownership and boundary enforcement; the documented splits were made at a traffic wall or at hundreds of teams and took years, so a merchant's own code gets one deployment unit per team that must release independently, with boundaries drawn around systems of record.

A hosted platform and every SaaS a merchant rents pool tenants and protect shared capacity with rate limits per app, store or customer that the vendor may lower; the merchant plans its share: who spends each budget, the order flow first at peak, and one tenant for several markets while the platform can vary what differs.

Extension mechanisms differ by where the code runs, what it may touch and how tightly it is tied to the vendor's releases; app review cannot see two apps writing one fact, so the merchant keeps an owner, scopes and API version per app, one writer per fact, and custom behavior out of the core.

The storefront renders facts other systems own and leaves checkout on the platform under every rendering model; content is cached and promises are fetched or validated live, and headless pays only for a need the theme cannot meet, with a team to run it, never for speed alone.

The platform smooths its peak across merchants while the merchant's chain meets its own spike alone; the merchant measures every link in orders per minute, tests above the forecast, protects checkout with gauged queues and a written switch-off order, and reconciles its systems the morning after.

flow.rationale: The page states a problem and the part's answer. It opens on a hosted platform that keeps taking orders while the merchant's connector falls behind (the problem: which part limits the order flow); places the part inside the platforms Part VI's joins attach to; gives Kestrel & Pine's case, two rebuild proposals aimed at the shop platform that held while the merchant's joins failed; then the claim, that the vendor's inside reaches the merchant as limits and the promises are kept or broken in the merchant's own layer; then the five questions the chapters ask, one per layer, with their figure; then one paragraph per chapter; and a closing that reads the opening scene along the part's line and says where to start. The case comes before the claim because the claim answers it; the five questions come after the claim because each asks where the vendor's limits end and the merchant's layer begins for one layer, and they sit directly before the chapter list that answers them. Put the claim first and it answers a problem the reader has not seen; put the questions before the claim and their reading order arrives before the reader knows what is being read (both round 2 flow readers).
